title: White Dwarfs: Electron Degeneracy Pressure and the Chandrasekhar Limit
executive_summary: A white dwarf is a stellar core remnant composed mostly of electron-degenerate matter. A white dwarf is very dense: its mass is comparable to that of the Sun, while its volume is comparable to that of Earth.
image_caption: Sirius B (lower left), a famous white dwarf orbiting Sirius A.

key_sections.title: Electron Degeneracy Pressure
key_sections.content: White dwarfs are supported against gravitational collapse by electron degeneracy pressure—a quantum mechanical effect described by the Pauli Exclusion Principle, which prevents identical electrons from occupying the same quantum state.

key_sections.title: The Chandrasekhar Limit (1.44 Solar Masses)
key_sections.content: The Chandrasekhar Limit is the maximum mass threshold (~1.44 M_sun) for a stable white dwarf. If a white dwarf accretes matter beyond this limit, electron degeneracy pressure fails, triggering a runaway thermonuclear Type Ia Supernova.

key_sections.title: Cooling Curves and Black Dwarfs
key_sections.content: Because white dwarfs no longer generate nuclear fusion energy, they slowly radiate their residual heat into space over hundreds of billions of years, eventually cooling into hypothetical cold 'black dwarfs'.
